interest: This document offers valuable insight into Japanese psychological warfare and radio propaganda targeting South Asia during the later stages of World War II. It illustrates how Axis broadcasters seized upon real-time domestic political friction in Ceylon—specifically the Board of Ministers' dispute with the British Colonial Office and the planned boycott of the constitutional reform commission—to stimulate anti-colonial agitation. Additionally, it highlights American diplomatic surveillance of Axis attempts to tie the United States directly to British imperialism and resource exploitation across Asia.
overview: This file comprises Confidential Despatch No. 608, dated September 25, 1944, from American Consul Robert L. Buell in Colombo, Ceylon, to the U.S. Secretary of State, along with its enclosed monitoring report of Japanese radio propaganda directed at Ceylon between September 3 and September 22, 1944. Monitored by the Ceylon Department of Information from stations such as Free India (Saigon), Radio Singapore, and Free Lanka Radio, the broadcasts actively exploited local political grievances—notably the Ceylon Board of Ministers' withdrawal of reform proposals and protests against the incoming British Royal Commission—to urge a united front and boycott against British rule. The propaganda contrasted British reluctance to grant self-government with Japan's nominal grants of independence to Burma, the Philippines, and Java, while promoting Subhas Chandra Bose and the Indian National Army as liberators. Buell noted that the broadcasts sought to tar the United States with responsibility for British colonial exploitation, though he assessed that very few listeners in Ceylon actually received the transmissions.

subfiles.about: Cover despatch from the American Consulate in Colombo forwarding monitored Japanese radio propaganda directed at Ceylon.
subfiles.summary: American Consul Robert L. Buell transmits excerpts from monitoring bulletins of the Ceylon Department of Information covering Japanese radio broadcasts beamed to Ceylon from September 3 to September 22, 1944. Buell highlights Japan's propaganda efforts to contrast its own grants of independence in Southeast Asia with British delays in expanding self-government in Ceylon. He observes that the broadcasts deliberately invoke 'Anglo-American' policies to make the United States appear co-responsible for British colonial rule. Buell concludes that although few in Ceylon listen to these broadcasts, they demonstrate Japan's propaganda approach toward Asian dependencies.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 608 from Robert L. Buell on Japanese Propaganda Broadcasts Directed to Ceylon

subfiles.about: Excerpts from monitoring bulletins transcribing Japanese propaganda broadcasts directed at Ceylon from Saigon, Singapore, and Free Lanka Radio.
subfiles.summary: This enclosure contains monitored summaries and transcripts of seven Japanese and Axis propaganda radio transmissions broadcast between September 3 and September 22, 1944, targeting audiences in Ceylon. The broadcasts seized upon local political developments, such as the Board of Ministers withdrawing their constitutional proposals and calls to boycott the British Royal Commission, urging the Sinhalese and minority communities to mount a united anti-British front. They accused the Anglo-American forces of exploiting Ceylon's foodstuffs and transportation, referenced speeches by Ceylonese leader D. S. Senanayake, and contrasted British oppression with Japanese support for Burma, Java, and the Philippines. Additionally, broadcasts from Free Lanka Radio promoted Subhas Chandra Bose and the Indian National Army, promising that armed forces would arrive to liberate Ceylon once the monsoon rains subsided.
subfiles.title: Enclosure to Despatch No. 608: Monitored Japanese Broadcasts Referring to Ceylon (September 3-22, 1944)
